variants.name: std::variant event contract with std::visit dispatch
variants.implementation_notes: std::variant<Types...> gives the event contract as a value-semantic tagged union - no event base class, no heap allocation per event, no RTTI - and std::visit dispatches to one overload per alternative, replacing the virtual dispatch of the classic hierarchy. What C++ does not provide is the other half of the pattern: there is no standard serialisation for a variant and no channel, so the wire form needs a library (protobuf/FlatBuffers) or hand-written framing, and delivery is a hand-written subscriber container, a Boost.Signals2 signal or a broker client. Prefer std::variant (C++17) whenever the events stay in-process; cross the process boundary with a schema-declared message type instead, because a variant cannot describe a stable wire format on its own.
variants.idiom_name: std::variant event contract + std::visit dispatch on a hand-written bus
pitfalls: std::visit needs an overload for every alternative; a generic fallback lambda silences the compile error that would have caught a new event type nobody handles.
The subscriber container must not be mutated while publish() iterates it; copy the subscriber list or use a stable registry.
A variant event is only as cheap as its largest alternative - avoid embedding large payload structs by value; box them or hold ids.

variants.name: Schema-declared event message over a broker
variants.implementation_notes: The variant cannot cross a process boundary, so the wire realization is schema-declared: one protobuf message per event type plus an envelope (or broker headers) carrying the type id and timestamp; the generated classes are the event payload, and the consumer switches on the type id and parses the corresponding message. This is the C++ form of the EIP pattern proper - the .proto file is the public contract, and field numbers, reserved tags and unknown-field retention provide the forward/backward compatibility the classic hand-written structs never had. Choose it when events leave the process; keep std::variant for the in-process channel and generate one from the other only at the seam.
variants.idiom_name: protobuf/FlatBuffers message per event type + envelope, delivered by a broker client
pitfalls: Field numbers are permanent once messages are in flight; deleting or renumbering a field corrupts or loses data for existing consumers - reserve retired numbers.
Serialising from the domain model directly bakes internal fields into the public contract; map to a dedicated message type at the boundary.
Per-message heap allocation and copy on publish is a real cost at high event rates; FlatBuffers or arena allocation avoids it when the rate justifies the complexity.
